Sort of. It's not hard to claim to be a country, the hard part is getting recognition and not being invaded by someone with bigger guns. A group around 30 years ago took an unclaimed coral atoll called Minerva and used landfill to raise it's surface above the water, thus making it dry land and eligable for making a territorial claim (which they did). Tonga invaded and kicked them all off. They then got into a territorial dispute with fiji until all the sand washed away and it became international waters again.

It would be tempting to pick one of those parcels of land and attempt to found a sovereign nation, but as an unrecognised country you would not be considered a legal entity in any dispute over the land and you would be unable to make any protest if one of your neighbours claimed the territory.

Still cool to see some of the world hasn't been nabbed yet though.

Yes, invasion would be a very big problem for an unrecognized country. Just look at all the border disputes of recognized countries. On the other side, if land is not officially claimed today it's probably of negative worth.

Sealand failed, but I'd love it if the were some floats (like from snow crash by stephenson) to claim to be countries and see what happens.

>On the other side, if land is not officially claimed today it's probably of negative worth.

I think it's more because of oversights and bitter disputes between neighbours not making it worthwhile to get into a legal (or actual) battle over. Take Bir Tawil for example, neither Sudan nor Egypt claim it because doing so would mean giving up their claims on the much larger Hala'ib triangle. But if a third party came in and tried to claim it they would likely move quickly to reach an agreement and file a counterclaim. I'm not sure I'd like to become the rope in a tug of war between two nations.

Sealand didn't really fail as such, they even got some de-facto recognition when the Netherlands negotiated with them to release two of their citizens (who had invaded). Sealand's problem was the lack of interest, only two or three people wanted to live there. I suspect they could have gotten more if they hadn't structured it as a monarchy, maybe invited some anarcho syndicalists in? But I think their intention was more to have it as a gimick than to try and seriously build a functional community.
